title: B2B Ecommerce Platform Migration 2026: An APAC Buyer's Guide
summary: A practical 2026 buyer guide to B2B ecommerce platform migration for APAC companies: evaluation criteria, real pricing, a scoring framework and timelines.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Evaluate a 2026 B2B migration on pricing-engine fidelity and ERP integration first, not storefront design. Expect three-year TCO of US$640K (Shopify Plus) to US$1.7M (composable) for a regional distributor, and six to nine months for a multi-market cutover.


---


Start at the end. Twelve months after cutover, a successful B2B ecommerce platform migration in 2026 looks like this: 60–70% of reorder volume comes in through self-service instead of email and WhatsApp, your inside sales team spends its day on new accounts rather than typing PO numbers, contract pricing resolves correctly for every tier without a human checking it, and your ERP is the single source of truth for stock and credit limits. Nobody talks about the platform any more, because it stopped being a topic.

*Related reading:*[Shopify vs Adobe Commerce APAC 2026: The Honest Verdict](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-vs-adobe-commerce-apac-2026)


*Related reading:*[Ecommerce Platform Comparison APAC 2026: 15 Platforms Ranked](https://branch8.com/posts/ecommerce-platform-comparison-apac-2026)


Now work backwards. Almost every failure mode I've seen in APAC replatforming projects — Hong Kong distributors, Taiwanese manufacturers with dealer networks, Singapore-headquartered regional wholesalers — traces back to a decision made in the evaluation phase, not the build phase. The platform was chosen on demo quality. Pricing logic was treated as a configuration detail. ERP integration was scoped as "phase two." The migration technically shipped, and then order volume stayed on email.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Snowflake Real-Time CDP Integration for APAC Retail](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-snowflake-real-time-cdp-integration-apac-retail)


*Related reading:*[Google Gemma 4 Offline iPhone AI Inference for APAC Retail](https://branch8.com/posts/google-gemma-4-offline-iphone-ai-inference-apac-retail)


This guide is written for the evaluation phase: what to score, what it costs, and how long it actually takes.


## The Market Backdrop Worth Knowing Before You Budget


The demand signal is real. Analyst estimates put the global B2B ecommerce market at roughly US$24 trillion in 2025 heading toward US$28 trillion in 2026 (figures circulated from Statista and Grand View Research aggregations), and Shopify reported that B2B GMV on its platform grew 96% year-over-year in 2025 as B2B capability rolled out beyond Plus-only tiers. Statista-sourced estimates cited across the replatforming market put 2025 B2B migration spend near US$4.2 billion.


Two things follow from that for APAC buyers specifically.


First, the platform vendors have finally shipped native B2B primitives — company accounts, buyer hierarchies, catalog- and customer-specific price lists, quote workflows — that used to require custom builds or a dedicated B2B suite. That collapses the cost floor for a mid-market replatform considerably compared to 2021.


Second, capability is not evenly distributed across the region. A platform that handles US ACH and net-30 terms elegantly may have nothing for Hong Kong FPS, Taiwan ATM virtual accounts, Japanese *konbini* settlement, Indonesian VA transfers, or Australian e-invoicing under the Peppol framework the ATO has been pushing. Your 2026 shortlist should be filtered by payment and invoicing reality in your top three markets before anyone looks at a demo.


## Nine Evaluation Criteria That Predict Post-Launch Outcomes


These are ordered by how often they cause pain after cutover, not by how much airtime they get in sales decks.


### 1. Pricing and entitlement engine depth


B2B pricing is rarely "a discount on retail." It is customer-specific price lists, volume break tiers, contracted item pricing with expiry dates, promotional overlays, currency-specific lists, and rounding rules that differ by market. Test with your own worst account — the one with 400 negotiated SKUs across three currencies.


Ask specifically: where does price get calculated? A platform that resolves price locally from synced price lists behaves very differently from one that calls the ERP in real time. Real-time calls are accurate and slow; synced lists are fast and go stale. Both are valid. Pick knowingly.


### 2. ERP and master-data integration model


The integration determines your run cost for the next five years. Score three things: whether the platform exposes bulk APIs (not just per-record REST), whether it supports webhooks or event streams for order and inventory deltas, and whether there is a maintained connector for your ERP version — SAP S/4HANA, Business Central, NetSuite, or the regional favourites like Kingdee and Yonyou in Greater China.


A Shopify B2B catalog price query looks like this, and the shape of it tells you a lot about how much translation logic your middleware will carry:


```text
1  query companyPrices($companyLocationId: ID!, $first: Int!) {    2    companyLocation(id: $companyLocationId) {    3      name    4      currency    5      catalogs(first: 5) {    6        nodes {    7          title    8          priceList {    9            currency    10            prices(first: $first) {    11              nodes {    12                variant { sku }    13                price { amount currencyCode }    14                compareAtPrice { amount }    15              }    16            }    17          }    18        }    19      }    20    }    21  }
```


If your ERP holds 90,000 SKU-customer price combinations, ask the vendor for the documented write throughput on their bulk price-list endpoints and the rate limits. Get it in writing before contract, not during UAT.


### 3. Buyer identity and account hierarchy


Real B2B buying involves a head-office account, multiple ship-to locations, a purchasing user who can only draft orders, an approver with a spend ceiling, and a finance user who only sees invoices. If the platform models this as "customer tags," you are going to build it yourself.


### 4. Quote-to-order and offline order capture


In most APAC dealer networks, a meaningful share of orders will keep starting as a conversation. The platform needs draft orders, sales-rep-on-behalf-of ordering, and quote expiry — otherwise your sales team routes around the system and your adoption metric dies quietly.


### 5. Multi-store, multi-currency, multi-entity structure


A Singapore holding company selling into Malaysia, Indonesia, and Australia usually needs separate legal entities, tax treatments, and price books but shared catalog data. Ask how many storefronts are included in the base licence and what the marginal cost of entity number four is. This is where quoted pricing and actual pricing diverge most often.


### 6. Search and catalog scale


B2B catalogs are deep, ugly, and searched by part number. Test with your real SKU file: 50,000+ variants, alphanumeric part codes, customer-specific catalog visibility, and traditional Chinese, simplified Chinese, and English product names in the same index. Native search on most platforms will not survive this; budget for Algolia, Elasticsearch, or the vendor's premium search tier.


### 7. Composable versus monolithic — decided by team, not fashion


Headless and composable architecture is genuinely better for organisations that have, or will hire, front-end engineers. It is genuinely worse for organisations of four marketers who need to change a banner on Friday afternoon. The API-first trend is real — Elastic Path, commercetools and others have made it the default enterprise narrative for 2026 — but the operating cost is a permanent front-end team.


My honest heuristic: if you cannot name the two engineers who will own your storefront repository twelve months after launch, buy the monolith with a good theme layer.


### 8. Data residency, PDPA/PIPL and audit posture


If you sell into mainland China, PIPL cross-border transfer rules matter. Singapore's PDPA, Australia's Privacy Act reforms, and Hong Kong's PDPO all shape where customer and pricing data can sit. Ask which regions the vendor runs production data in and whether they will contract to it. Several global SaaS platforms serve APAC from US or EU regions by default.


### 9. Partner availability in your time zone


Underrated and expensive. A platform with three certified implementation partners in APAC and a nine-hour support gap will cost you more in delay than any licence saving. Check the vendor's partner directory filtered by your country before shortlisting.

## What a 2026 Replatform Actually Costs


Three cost layers: licence, implementation, and run. Buyers routinely model the first and underestimate the other two by half.


### Platform licence, annual


**Shopify Plus** publishes pricing — from US$2,300/month on a three-year term, or US$2,500/month on a one-year commitment, per Shopify's Plus pricing page, with variable platform fees applying above defined GMV thresholds. B2B features (company accounts, price lists, payment terms) are included rather than a separate SKU. Call it roughly US$28,000–US$45,000/year for a mid-market B2B operation once you add apps.


**Adobe Commerce** does not publish list pricing. Partner- and buyer-reported annual licence figures cluster broadly between US$40,000 and US$190,000, tiered by GMV band, with Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service adding managed infrastructure into the same commitment. Adobe's B2B module capability is deep — shared catalogs, requisition lists, company hierarchies — which is why it still wins complex distributor tenders.


**BigCommerce Enterprise** sits between the two, typically negotiated in the US$1,500–US$6,000/month band depending on order volume and storefront count, with B2B Edition bundling in quote and price-list tooling.


**commercetools and other composable backends** generally start in the low-to-mid six figures annually for enterprise contracts, priced on API calls and orders. That is before front-end hosting (Vercel or Netlify, typically US$500–US$3,000/month at B2B traffic levels), a CMS such as Contentful or Sanity, search, and a PIM.


**SHOPLINE** is the interesting regional case. Its published SMB plans run from a few hundred HKD per month, with enterprise and O2O packages negotiated. For Greater China B2B operators who need native WeChat, Alipay, FPS and Taiwan payment rails plus local-language merchant support, the total cost of getting to the same functional place is often materially lower than porting a Western stack into the region.


**SAP Commerce Cloud and Salesforce B2B Commerce** remain the choice where the ERP or CRM relationship dominates. Salesforce has historically priced B2B Commerce partly on a percentage of GMV — model that carefully, because a GMV-linked fee on a US$200M distribution business is a very different number from a flat licence.


### Implementation


Based on APAC tenders and scopes we see, realistic ranges for a genuine B2B replatform:


- **Straightforward mid-market** (one entity, one currency, one ERP, ~5,000 SKUs, standard price lists): US$80,000–US$180,000.
- **Regional multi-entity** (3–5 markets, multi-currency, dealer hierarchy, custom approval flows, 30,000+ SKUs): US$200,000–US$500,000.
- **Composable enterprise** (headless front end, PIM, middleware layer, two-way ERP sync, phased dealer rollout): US$500,000–US$1.5M+.


These are estimates of market range, not guaranteed outcomes. The single biggest swing factor is not design or front-end work — it is how clean your product and pricing master data is. A distributor with 40,000 SKUs and no consistent attribute schema will spend more on data remediation than on the storefront.


### Run cost, year two onward


Budget 15–25% of implementation cost annually for maintenance, integration monitoring, platform version upgrades, and iteration. Composable stacks land at the top of that range or above, because you own more moving parts. Skipping this line item is how organisations end up on a five-year-old build that nobody will touch.


### A three-year TCO sketch


For a regional distributor doing US$40M annual B2B revenue across four APAC markets:


- Shopify Plus route: licence ~US$120K, apps ~US$60K, implementation ~US$280K, run ~US$180K → roughly **US$640K over three years** .
- Adobe Commerce route: licence ~US$330K, implementation ~US$420K, run ~US$260K → roughly **US$1.01M over three years** .
- Composable route: backend + services ~US$600K, implementation ~US$700K, run ~US$400K → roughly **US$1.7M over three years** .


The question is never which is cheapest. It is whether the incremental US$400K buys pricing logic, entity structure, or catalog depth you genuinely cannot get one tier down.


## A Weighted Scoring Framework You Can Run in a Week


Use 100 points. Weight to your business, but this allocation reflects where post-launch failures actually originate.


### Weightings


- **Pricing and entitlement fidelity — 20 points.** Can it express your worst contract without custom code?
- **ERP and data integration — 18 points.** Connector maturity, bulk API throughput, event support.
- **Buyer account and permission model — 12 points.** Hierarchies, approvals, roles.
- **Regional payments, tax and invoicing — 12 points.** Your top three markets only.
- **Catalog and search at your scale — 10 points.** Tested with your real SKU export.
- **Total three-year cost of ownership — 10 points.** Licence plus implementation plus run.
- **Team fit and operating model — 8 points.** Who maintains it, and can they?
- **APAC partner and support depth — 6 points.** Certified partners in-region, support hours.
- **Extensibility and exit cost — 4 points.** Data portability, API completeness.


### Scoring discipline


Score each criterion 0–5 and multiply by the weight, but apply two rules that stop the exercise from becoming theatre.


**Rule one: veto gates.** Any platform scoring 0–1 on pricing fidelity or regional payments is eliminated regardless of total. A high total with a fatal gap is the most expensive outcome available.


**Rule two: score from artefacts, not demos.** A score of 4 or 5 requires evidence — a sandbox you loaded your own data into, a documented API limit, a reference customer in your region and sector. Vendor assertions cap at 3.


### Interpretation bands


- **80+** — proceed to a paid discovery sprint with that platform's partner.
- **65–79** — viable, but list the gaps and price them as custom scope before committing.
- **Below 65** — you are buying a build project wearing a platform's badge.

## Timeline and Sequencing for a 2026 Cutover


Searches around "B2B ecommerce platform migration 2026 dates" usually mean one thing: when do we start to be live before peak? For most APAC B2B businesses, peak is Q4 buying plus Lunar New Year pre-stocking, which means the safe cutover windows are roughly March–May or August–September.


A realistic phasing for a regional multi-entity migration:


**Weeks 1–4 — Discovery and data audit.** Export your product master, price lists, and customer hierarchy. Count the exceptions. This phase determines everything downstream, and rushing it is the most common self-inflicted wound.


**Weeks 5–8 — Architecture and integration design.** Decide where price is calculated, where stock is authoritative, and what happens when the ERP is down. Write the failure behaviour down.


**Weeks 9–20 — Build and integration.** Storefront, catalog, pricing sync, order flow, invoice and payment rails per market.


**Weeks 21–26 — Data migration and UAT with real buyers.** Not internal staff. Get eight actual purchasing managers, including the one who complains most, ordering in staging.


**Weeks 27–28 — Pilot cutover with one market or one dealer segment.** Then SEO redirect mapping, which is where the second-most-cited failure mode lives — 301 mapping every legacy URL, preserving gated category structure, and re-verifying in Search Console.


**Weeks 29–52 — Rollout and adoption.** The part nobody budgets. Buyer onboarding, sales team incentive alignment, and killing the email ordering channel deliberately rather than hoping it fades.


Six to nine months is normal for a serious multi-market B2B migration. Anyone quoting eight weeks is quoting a theme install.


## Where These Projects Fail After Launch


The uncomfortable pattern — and the industry commentary in 2025–26 has converged on this — is that B2B migrations rarely fail at cutover. They fail in month three.


**Pricing drift.** Sync jobs fail silently, a customer sees list price instead of contract price, and trust is gone. Instrument this: a scheduled job that reconciles a sample of ERP prices against platform prices daily and alerts on variance. Something as simple as this belongs in every B2B build:


```text
1  # nightly price reconciliation, exits non-zero on drift    2  curl -s -H "X-Shopify-Access-Token: $TOKEN" \    3    "https://$SHOP/admin/api/2026-01/price_lists/$LIST_ID/prices.json?limit=250" \    4    | jq -r '.prices[] | [.variant_id, .price.amount] | @csv' > platform_prices.csv    5
6  python3 reconcile.py --erp erp_export.csv --platform platform_prices.csv \    7    --tolerance 0.01 --alert-webhook "$SLACK_HOOK"
```


**Adoption stall.** Buyers registered but never reordered. The fix is operational, not technical: sales compensation tied to portal orders, and a hard date after which email POs get a polite redirect.


**Integration decay.** The ERP gets patched, a field changes, the connector breaks, and nobody notices for a week because there is no alerting on the middleware.


We worked with a Greater China industrial distributor selling through a multi-tier dealer network where the entire evaluation had focused on storefront design. The pricing hierarchy — dealer tier, then annual volume commitment, then project-specific override — had lived in spreadsheets maintained by three regional managers. The platform decision was straightforward once that logic was documented; the six weeks spent documenting it was the actual project. That sequencing lesson generalises: model the pricing before you shortlist the platform.

## Using Asia as the Operations Layer, Not Just a Market


For US and European B2B companies, there is a structural argument for running the APAC commerce build from within the region. Payment rails, invoicing compliance, and language handling are local problems that are cheaper to solve locally. Singapore and Hong Kong give you English-language contracting, common-law frameworks, and time-zone overlap with the manufacturing base in Vietnam, Taiwan, and southern China. Australia and New Zealand add mature e-invoicing infrastructure through Peppol.


Running the same stack from a US headquarters usually produces one of two outcomes: a global template that fits no APAC market well, or a series of country exceptions that quietly become five separate codebases. The middle path — one platform, regionally-owned configuration, one integration layer — is harder to set up and much cheaper to run.


## How to Evaluate: Your Next Four Weeks


A B2B ecommerce platform migration in 2026 is a data and process project with a storefront attached. Run the evaluation accordingly.


**Week 1 — Export your reality.** Product master, full price-list matrix, customer hierarchy, twelve months of orders split by channel. Count how many orders currently arrive by email or messaging app. That number is your business case.


**Week 2 — Write the pricing specification.** Every rule, every exception, every override, with an owner's name against each. If this document is under four pages, you have not finished.


**Week 3 — Load your own data into two or three sandboxes.** Not the vendor's demo catalog. Yours. Score against the weighted framework, applying the veto gates and the artefact rule.


**Week 4 — Price three-year TCO for the top two, including run cost and the marginal cost of market number four.** Then choose on the difference in capability, not the difference in licence.


If the exercise tells you your current platform is fine and the problem is data quality and sales process, that is a legitimate outcome — and a much cheaper year.
